Learning Objectives
Apply continuous performance improvement and skill enhancement, which are critical to a life-
long practice of excellence within the field of orthopaedic surgery.
Build a habit of setting clear goals, practicing skills in the sweet spot, maximizing engagement,
finding areas for improvement, and seeking feedback.
Identify with and incorporate the concepts of continuous performance improvement into daily
practice.
Introduction and Definitions
Performance improvement requires focused skill development within multiple domains.

Although much of performance improvement has been considered anecdotal or inexact,
additional clarity has been obtained via recent research efforts.
Process improvement refers to the act of transformation of health care toward higher quality
and lower costs.
Skills comprise all the facets of the practice of an orthopaedic surgeon, including but not
limited to the vast array of surgical skills required of the profession.
Improving Skills and Performance
Skill development encompasses the process of goal setting, deliberate practice, and focus on
results.1
Hard skills are those that require precision and reproducibility.
Demand hard skill perfection in the operating room. These skills must always be consistent.
Surgical knot-tying is an example of a hard skill.
Find a practice mode and take chances to refine your techniques in this setting.
For example, many surgical trainees refine their surgical knot-tying techniques on a knot-
tying board long before they are tying surgical knots in the operating room.
No hard skill more important for any surgeon than mastering the basics. The most basic hard
skill is a comprehensive understanding of anatomy.
Extreme knowledge of anatomy serves as a surgeon’s protection.
Nothing changes a surgeon’s behavior more than detailed knowledge of anatomy.
Review anatomy on a regular basis. Talented surgeons always achieve great exposure
because of their knowledge of anatomy and then make the surgery look elegant and easy.
Soft skills are those that are more improvisational and require decision making based on the
best available information at the time.
Soft skills require surgeons to read, recognize, and react in a controlled and focused fashion.
Mastering soft skills requires surgeons to behave decisively, be curious, and experiment with
new methods that challenge themselves and their minds.
The future is not easily predictable; however, the more scenarios that are visualized and
reacted to ahead of time, the better prepared a surgeon will be.
Never stop asking “what if this happens?”2
Anticipating possible intraoperative complications and having the appropriate tools and
instruments to manage the complication is critical and necessary preparation for any surgical
procedure.
Deliberate practice

This term, popularized by Professor Anders Ericsson, details the methodologic process of
gaining improvement in a given skill.
The quality of deliberate practice is overwhelmingly more important than the amount of time
spent practicing.3
Focused practice, with continuous quality reaches, repetitions, feedback, and correction, is
more important than the number of hours dedicated to the practice.
Reach further, maximize effort, focus during practice, and solicit and respond to feedback.
Practice begins when a surgeon gets it right. If a surgeon gets it right, do it correctly five
more times to lock it in before celebrating.
Make surgical practice the game, and do not fall into the trap of leisurely surgical
procedures.
Struggle is the biologic ingredient for skill to blossom. The brain works in a manner similar
to the muscles: no pain, no gain.
Put effort into making excellence a habit in all aspects of skills. Begin by obsessing over
perfect surgical positioning and draping.
Fundamental tenets of deliberate practice include the following:
Expertise is not solely based on innate talent or time spent on a skill but is dependent on
intensive, guided practice.
The velocity of skill acquisition and performance enhancement is proportional to the
amount of time spent practicing in the sweet spot.
The sweet spot is reached after a surgeon put himself or herself at the edge of his or her
ability, which is the point at which a surgeon learns the best and the most quickly.
Push to find the sweet spot with every aspect of any skill desired to improve on.
Skill acquisition also is subject to the compounding effect. Regular focused effort-filled
practice early in a surgeon’s career and training leads to exponential gains over time.
Deconstruct the skill into the smallest possible subskills (a process known as chunking).4
Learn each subskill.
Remove any physical, mental, and emotional barriers that obstruct practice.
Practice the most important subskills.
The development of clear goals followed by the development of a process and a timeline to
achieve them is critical.
One helpful system is to use the SMART goals acronym for individual goals.
Specific—Set extremely specific goals and attach numbers to them if appropriate.
Measurable—Ensure the goal can be tracked and monitored.

Attainable—Work toward challenging but attainable goals.
Realistic—Be honest about capabilities.
Time-bound—Provide a deadline to achieve the goal, and maintain accountability.
Importance of real-time feedback and coaching
Reflect on the engagement immediately afterward with an after-action review.
Surgeons should give themselves a letter grade at the completion of every surgical
procedure; make it harsh, and foster self-critique.
Leave ego at the door and make self-critique the most powerful surgical mastery tool.
Decide what went wrong and why. Forming solutions is better than simply acknowledging
problems.
Overcome and rise above circumstantial limitations. Do not blame what cannot be controlled
because it wastes precious time, energy, and focus.
Top performers never blame others or circumstances for poor performance.
Grit is defined as “perseverance and passion for long-term goals” and is one of the most
important attributes that keep individuals moving forward despite obstacles.5
Write down a plan for execution of the next surgical procedures, practice, or challenge and the
expected result before the engagement.
Mentally rehearse every step of the engagement from the moment.
Mental imagery is a fully immersive multisensory procedure that associates numerous
senses to create a mental image and process it without the presence of external stimuli. It
has been shown to be an effective method to improve learning, performance, and other
results in athletic and non-athletic populations.6,7
The REPS acronym is helpful in critically assessing a surgeon’s own practice.
Reaching and repeating
Does the practice have a surgeon operating on the edge of his or her ability, reaching, and
repeating?
Always find the sweet spot in practice.
Engagement
Is the practice immersive?
Does it use emotion to propel the surgeon toward a goal?
Embrace the struggle and strive to be better than the masters.
Get the most possible intensity out of any training environment.
Purposefulness
Does the task directly connect to the desired skill?

Use self-reflection to determine areas most in need of improvement and areas most critical
to performance.
Align purpose with goals.
Strong, speedy feedback
Does the learner receive a stream of accurate information about his or her performance—
successes and mistakes?
Feedback must be constantly available.
Lack of feedback is like a chef trying to improve without ever tasting the food.
Continuing education is vital for developing and sustaining the skills required for the life-long
practice of excellence within the field of orthopaedic surgery.
Seek out and capitalize on opportunities to attend cadaver laboratories, courses, and
academic meetings to broaden knowledge and skill base.
Staying up to date with regular reading and note-taking from academic journals is required
to stay informed.
Society involvement will expose surgeons to other like-minded high-level performers who will
push and challenge each other to deliver the highest level of care to patients.
Process Improvement
Current shift to value-based health care (from volume-based care) has placed focus on process
improvement.
The ultimate goal is to provide improved quality and lower-cost health care.
Requires understanding of key drivers of quality along with metrics by which to measure
success
Recent summary of improvement essentials as outlined by Press Ganey
Define organizational strategy toward true north mission to align improvement efforts.
Vertical deployment of strategy throughout the organization
Focus on implementation of lean-related tools.
Invest in leadership development to align goals.
Integrate daily management systems for practical execution of strategies and initiatives.
Participation across the organization in development and training activities
Plan-Do-Study-Act framework8
Tool for documenting change
Develop a plan to test the change.
Carry out the test (do).

Observe and learn from the consequences (study).
Determine the modifications necessary to the test (act).
Donabedian framework for process improvement
“Process denotes what is actually done in giving and receiving care. It includes the patient’s
activities in seeking care and carrying it out as well as the practitioner’s activities in making a
diagnosis and recommending or implementing a treatment.”9
Process encompasses the sum of actions comprising health care, consisting of technical
processes (care delivery) and interpersonal processes (manner of care delivery).
